albert_park.description: Set in Melbourne, this non-permanent street circuit offers fast corners and very little margin for error. A technical track that demands an excellent aerodynamic balance.
albert_park.trivia: As a public park for the rest of the year, the track is notoriously slippery and 'green' at the start of the weekend. Before F1 arrives, its roads are used every day by Melbourne commuters.

shanghai.description: Famous for its iconic 'snail' first corner that never seems to end and for the very long back straight where the cars unleash every horsepower of their power unit.
shanghai.trivia: The layout is inspired by the Chinese character 'Shang' (上), meaning 'to rise'. The track was also built on top of a swamp, which made the engineering work colossal.

suzuka.description: The only figure-of-eight circuit in F1. A technical masterpiece loved by every driver, with its famous first sector of lightning-fast esses and the feared 130R.
suzuka.trivia: Originally designed by John Hugenholtz as a Honda test track, Suzuka is also home to a large amusement park. The Ferris wheel overlooking the circuit has become one of Formula 1's historic symbols.

bahrain.description: Built in the Sakhir desert, this stop-and-go track punishes the brakes and rear traction out of the slow corners. The race runs under floodlights.
bahrain.trivia: To stop sand from the surrounding desert blowing onto the track and damaging the cars, the organisers spray a special adhesive resin on the sand around the circuit before every race weekend.

jeddah.description: The fastest street circuit in the world. It snakes along the Red Sea with blind corners taken at crazy speeds, turning qualifying into a real test of courage.
jeddah.trivia: It was built in record time, in less than a year, with work going on around the clock. It is the second-longest track on the calendar, beaten only by majestic Spa-Francorchamps.

miami.description: Built around the Hard Rock Stadium, it alternates very fast sections with a tight and tricky twisty part, all wrapped in Florida's vibrant and glamorous atmosphere.
miami.trivia: The famous 'fake marina' inside the track caused a stir on debut: the boats are real, but they sit on a solid surface painted to look like rippling blue water.

villeneuve.description: On Notre-Dame Island in Montreal, a very fast circuit with long straights broken up by demanding chicanes. Using the kerbs well is vital for a good lap time.
villeneuve.trivia: The notorious 'Wall of Champions' at the exit of the final chicane got its name in 1999, when three world champions crashed into it in a single weekend: Damon Hill, Michael Schumacher and Jacques Villeneuve.

monaco.description: The jewel in Formula 1's crown. The streets of the Principality make up the shortest, narrowest and slowest track of the year, where overtaking is almost impossible and qualifying is everything.
monaco.trivia: The manhole covers are welded shut before the race, because the ground effect generated by the floor of modern F1 cars is strong enough to rip them out of the tarmac.

catalunya.description: A track the teams know inside out. It combines high, medium and low-speed corners, making it the perfect test bench for judging how competitive the cars really are.
catalunya.trivia: Since 2023 the slow final chicane has been removed, returning the track to its original 1990s layout. Drivers now take the last two corners flat out, arriving on the straight at dizzying speeds.

red_bull_ring.description: Set among the mountains of Styria in Austria, this is a very short circuit, with laps often under 1 minute 10. Few straights, big elevation changes and hard braking zones that favour overtaking.
red_bull_ring.trivia: The track has changed name three times: born as the Österreichring, rebuilt as the A1-Ring in the late 1990s, it was finally bought, renovated and renamed by Dietrich Mateschitz for Red Bull.

silverstone.description: The cradle of British motorsport. Built on a former military airfield, it is famous for high-speed sequences such as Maggotts, Becketts and Chapel that put the drivers' necks to the test.
silverstone.trivia: Silverstone hosted the very first round of the Formula 1 World Championship in 1950. Its wide track still largely follows the old runways used by Second World War bombers.

spa.description: The University of Formula 1. Winding through the Ardennes forest in Belgium, it offers the famous and terrifying uphill Eau Rouge-Raidillon combination. The thoroughbred racers' favourite track.
spa.trivia: The weather is so unstable and the lap so long that it often pours in the first sector while the third stays completely dry and sunny, making tyre choice a strategic nightmare.

hungaroring.description: Just outside Budapest, it is often called 'a giant go-kart track'. Narrow, twisty and dusty, it gives the drivers no rest and rewards pure downforce over engine power.
hungaroring.trivia: Built in 1986, it was the first circuit to host a Formula 1 race behind the Iron Curtain during the Cold War. Overtaking is hard, yet it has produced memorable wins in the rain.

zandvoort.description: Nestled among the North Sea dunes, it is a wild old-school track. Its tight corners and two striking banked turns make it feel like a rollercoaster ride.
zandvoort.trivia: The famous Tarzan corner (Turn 1) is not named after the fictional character, but after a local farmer who agreed to give up his land for the circuit only if the first corner was named after him.

monza.description: The 'Temple of Speed'. No circuit in the world has straights this long, where cars run almost wingless to hit 350 km/h before braking hard for the historic chicanes.
monza.trivia: It has the highest average lap speed of the whole championship. Partly woven into the modern track, it still preserves the historic and frightening concrete banking built in 1922.

madring.description: The big novelty of 2026. A hybrid semi-street circuit winding through Madrid's IFEMA exhibition grounds and the Valdebebas area, combining city roads with purpose-built sections.
madring.trivia: This track breaks several moulds: it features steeply banked corners designed for overtaking and even a spectacular indoor section where the cars race straight through the exhibition halls.

sepang.description: The return of a classic. Designed by Hermann Tilke on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur, it pairs two very long parallel straights joined by a hairpin with wide, fast corners that are tough on tyres and brakes.
sepang.trivia: Humid heat and tropical downpours are part of its charm: in 2009 a storm forced the race to be stopped for good before half distance, and half points were awarded for the first time since 1991.

baku.description: A track of two extremes. On one side the endless 2.2 km straight along the Caspian Sea, perfect for slipstream overtakes; on the other the narrow, claustrophobic climb up to the medieval castle.
baku.trivia: Turn 8, which runs around the old city walls, is just 7.6 metres wide. It is the narrowest point of the entire Formula 1 calendar, leaving the drivers millimetre margins.

marina_bay.description: The original night race. In Singapore the stifling humidity and unforgiving walls make this the most demanding physical and mental challenge of the season. A Safety Car here is almost guaranteed.
marina_bay.trivia: During the race the cockpit can reach 60°C. Drivers can lose up to 3-4 kg in sweat over the gruelling two hours it takes to complete the 62 laps.

americas.description: The beating heart of F1 in the United States, in Austin, Texas. Inspired by the best sectors of European tracks, it peaks with the iconic, very wide uphill Turn 1 that opens up several overtaking lines.
americas.trivia: The climb from the start line to the apex of Turn 1 is a full 41 metres. Because of the unstable clay soil, the track is notorious for constantly developing tricky natural bumps.

rodriguez.description: In Mexico City, more than 2,200 metres above sea level. The thin air dramatically affects cooling and the engines' turbos and reduces aerodynamic efficiency, forcing teams to run huge wings.
rodriguez.trivia: The third sector runs right through the 'Foro Sol', a huge baseball stadium. Driving through the roar of 30,000 fans packed into those stands creates a one-of-a-kind atmosphere.

interlagos.description: A São Paulo classic. It runs anticlockwise over hilly ground that punishes the drivers' neck muscles. The downhill 'Senna S' after the start is a masterpiece for overtaking.
interlagos.trivia: Built between two artificial lakes (hence the name 'Interlagos'), it is known for wildly unpredictable weather, which has decided the world championship at the very last corner on countless occasions.

vegas.description: A super-fast street circuit under the dazzling lights of Sin City. Its highlight is the endless flat-out straight along the famous Strip, past Nevada's iconic casinos.
vegas.trivia: The Las Vegas race runs on Saturday night local time for maximum visual impact and international TV audiences. In November the Nevada desert nights get close to freezing, making it very hard to warm up the tyres.

losail.description: Built for MotoGP, in F1 it turns into a flowing run of very high-speed sweepers. The front-left tyre is put under devastating lateral stress for the whole lap.
losail.trivia: Lusail's floodlighting is gigantic and needs a huge network of independent generators. The lighting is so powerful and even across the track that it casts no shadows on the cars.

yas_marina.description: Abu Dhabi's spectacular season finale. The race starts at sunset and ends under the moon, with fast sectors followed by a technical section around the iconic W Hotel.
yas_marina.trivia: It is the only track in the world whose pit lane exit runs through a real underground tunnel. The circuit is an artificial paradise, designed so that luxury yachts can watch the race right next to the track.
